extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, mass communication researchers, and graduate students
extracted.subtask_description: Developing and applying a hierarchical theory of the influences on news/media content, and deriving hypotheses and research designs linking individual, organizational, extramedia, and ideological factors to content and effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct and inferred effects of content
rubrics_metrics.description: Some content may have an effect on people directly, without media use as an intervening variable (e.g., through interpersonal talk about media, producing effects above and beyond an individual's own media use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This domain expands effects models to include cases where content influences audiences indirectly via social discussion or other pathways rather than just via measured individual exposure; researchers should consider these pathways when linking content to effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate content and effects studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Effects studies should include variables about the specific media content people have been exposed to, not just overall exposure to a medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to measure content (instead measuring hours of TV or days reading a paper) equates all content within a medium and can obscure important causal relationships; integration will foster theory development specific to mass communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure exposure to specific content (not just medium)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that exposure to a medium is not equivalent to exposure to specific content within that medium (e.g., heavy TV viewing does not necessarily mean exposure to violent programs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research designs should ask about or otherwise measure what specific content respondents saw/read rather than relying on coarse measures like hours of viewing or days reading a newspaper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for content cycles and temporal variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Media content varies by day and cycle (e.g., newspaper size midweek vs Saturday, availability of sources over weekends), so content on one day is not equivalent to another day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should identify and control for predictable temporal cycles in content availability when comparing content or linking content to effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardize content analysis measures for reliability and validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Content analysis measures should be reliable and valid across many kinds of content; current standardization lags behind survey/experimental research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without standardized, comparable, and valid measures, content analyses from different studies may not be comparable or sensitive enough to detect important differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess audience awareness of influences on content
rubrics_metrics.description: Alongside exposure as an intervening variable, assess the extent to which audiences are aware (correctly or not) of factors that influence media content (e.g., perceived publisher ties to business).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience interpretations and actions (e.g., voting against a newspaper's endorsement because they perceive bias) can moderate effects and should be measured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify relative importance and contingent conditions of influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess which influences on media content are most important and identify those that are crucial contingent conditions for the effects under study; not all influences matter equally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some influences (e.g., ideology, market forces) may be decisive in certain contexts while routines or individual idiosyncrasies matter in others; studies should specify and test contingencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption: media content is socially created
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass media content is a socially created product, not a reflection of objective reality; many factors determine what is transmitted and how.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat content as constructed by social actors and structures rather than as transparent mirrors of events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption: mixed intentionality of influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Some influences on content are intentional and others occur as a byproduct of other actions (e.g., source availability creating apparent bias).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should distinguish between deliberate influence and structural or routine-driven outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption: understanding content is crucial to understanding effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding the nature of media content is crucial for understanding the nature and importance of content's effects on people and society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effects research that ignores content-specific measures risks missing causal connections between exposure and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption: inferability of influences from content
rubrics_metrics.description: From media content we can infer many of the factors that shaped it (e.g., language indicating writer attitudes, story selection indicating editor priorities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content analysis can be used diagnostically to reveal shaping forces, but such inferences should be made carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption: similar forces shape news and entertainment
rubrics_metrics.description: General forces (individual workers, routines, organizations, extramedia factors, ideology) that operate to shape news content also shape entertainment content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply cross-genre thinking when theorizing influence processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption: hierarchical ranking of influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Influences on media content can be ranked hierarchically from macrosystem-level ideological forces down to micro-level characteristics of individual workers; each level is constrained by higher levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theory and research should model multi-level influence chains (e.g., ideology → organizational goals → routines → individual role conception).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption: gatekeeping limits content
rubrics_metrics.description: Not everything eligible to be mass media content actually gets into the media; gatekeeping selects items from the universe of possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for selection processes (what is excluded as well as what is included) in content studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption: routines are efficiency mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Media routines develop to make the media worker's job more efficient, operating under audience expectations and source constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routines should be analyzed as practical constraints that shape regularities in content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption: owners hold ultimate power
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate power in a media organization comes from the owner; owners set direction and ultimate policies even if lower-level employees exert influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider ownership structure when tracing determinants of content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption: media control via financing and regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: All mass media are controlled in some way—through financing, direct government ownership, laws/regulations/licenses/taxes, or indirect ideological directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the mechanisms of control (direct vs. indirect) appropriate to ownership/regulatory context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: television contains high and stable violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Television content (news and entertainment) contains a high level of violence that is fairly consistent over time; crimes depicted are more likely violent than nonviolent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use longitudinal and program-level analysis to confirm stability and prevalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: gender and age representation disparities
rubrics_metrics.description: In media content, women and the aged appear less often than men and younger adults and are presented differently (e.g., women shown younger/inferior roles; women more likely victims; aged stereotyped).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content analyses should measure frequency and portrayal attributes (roles, power, victim/perpetrator status).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: news skews to the already prominent
rubrics_metrics.description: Most news concerns people who are already prominent; nonprominent people must often do something deviant to receive coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate selection biases favoring elites and prominence as a newsworthiness determinant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: official sources dominate news
rubrics_metrics.description: Most news comes from official (primarily governmental) channels; journalists will use other sources when available, but governmental/business sources are most accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure source types and accessibility in source analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: geographic coverage imbalance in U.S. states
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States, news coverage of a state is not proportional to population: coastal states are overcovered while Midwest states are undercovered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider geographic and regional biases when analyzing national news flows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: occupational status skew in TV characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Among television characters, there are more people with high-status than low-status jobs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code occupational/status variables when assessing representational equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: minorities underrepresented and stereotyped
rubrics_metrics.description: Minority characters and newscasters are generally underrepresented and portrayed stereotypically; portrayals reflect societal power relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess both representation quantity and qualitative stereotyping; acculturation and socioeconomic status affect prominence of minority newsmakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (individuals): education/major affects content
rubrics_metrics.description: Media workers who have a 'communication' college degree produce content with different characteristics than those with other majors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare content produced by journalists with different educational backgrounds to test assumed effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (individuals): background and power interact
rubrics_metrics.description: A journalist's background and personal characteristics affect media content in proportion to the amount of power the person holds within the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure both individual attributes and position/authority to detect conditional effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (individuals): similarity influences coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: People who are similar to a journalist will be covered differently from those who are dissimilar (e.g., women write about women differently than men).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate demographic congruence between reporters and subjects as a predictor of framing and selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (individuals): personal attitudes influence content (conditional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Media workers' personal attitudes affect the content they produce, contingent on their power and on the absence of strong routines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess contexts (assignment autonomy, strength of routines) in which personal attitudes translate into content differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (individuals): role conceptions shape coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists' role conceptions (interpreting, disseminating, adversarial) determine job definitions, what should be covered, and how it is covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include measures of professional role conception in studies linking individual beliefs to content outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (individuals): ethical perceptions influence behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: The more unethical media workers think an action is, the less likely they are to take part in it; lack of a required ethical code leads to disagreement about ethics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey ethical norms and perceived acceptability alongside content practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (links individuals↔routines): socialization increases conformity
rubrics_metrics.description: The longer people work for a media organization, the more socialized they are to its policies—stated and unstated—and the more they learn what the organization wants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tenure as an independent variable when testing conformity to organizational standards and routines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (links individuals↔routines): objectivity routine limits personal opinion in news
rubrics_metrics.description: Media workers are less likely to insert personal value judgments into straight news than in other content because the journalistic routine of objectivity overrules individual tendencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate content types (straight news vs features) when measuring individual influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (links individuals↔routines): routines increase content use and similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The more media workers follow organizational routines, the more likely their content is to be used; routines (gatekeeping, deadlines, inverted pyramid, objectivity) shape content form and selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize specific routines and measure their prevalence to predict content conformity and usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (links individuals↔routines): routinization increases perceived professionalism
rubrics_metrics.description: The more media workers learn and follow job routines, the more professional they are rated by co-workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include peer- or supervisor-rated professionalism as an outcome in socialization studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (links individuals↔routines): individual influence greater without routines
rubrics_metrics.description: On stories or subjects without established routines (e.g., early stages of an issue), individual factors will be relatively more influential than routines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare routine vs non-routine story contexts to estimate individual-level effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (routines): congruence with routines predicts coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Events congruent with media routines are more likely to be covered than discongruent events (e.g., off-beat news, lack of footage may reduce likelihood).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess congruence of events with beats, deadlines, footage requirements, and definitions of newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (routines): events favored over issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Events are more likely to be covered than issues because events are more defensible and routine; covering events has itself become a routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish event-driven vs issue-driven coverage in content analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (routines): closeness to routine definition increases coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: The closer an event is to the organization's routine definition of newsworthiness, the more likely it will be covered; organizations value consistency over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure organizational definitions of newsworthiness and test their predictive power for selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (routines): pack journalism increases similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The more journalists cover an event, the more similar their coverage will be (pack journalism) due to shared ideas, confirmation, and editorial pressures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study inter-media similarity and confirmation-seeking behaviors among journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (routines): elite/powerful subjects receive more negative coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: The more powerful or successful people/groups are, the more negative news coverage they will receive (e.g., front-runners/incumbents receive more negative scrutiny).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test differential tone by power/status of subjects; consider investigative norms that target potential winners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (org↔routines): bureaucracy reduces professional routine influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The larger and more complex a media organization is, the less influence professional routines will have on content and the more influence larger organizational forces (economic concerns) will have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure organizational size/complexity and compare the relative impact of professional routines vs managerial economic priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (organizational): elite media staff more elite
rubrics_metrics.description: The more elite a medium is, the less similar its workers will be to the general population (e.g., elite news organization journalists are more liberal and from elite backgrounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine staff demographics and ideology by organizational prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (organizational): economic health conditions profit influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which an organization's need to make a profit affects content is contingent on its overall economic health; profitable organizations allow professional influences to prevail, whereas those at risk prioritize profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include organizational financial indicators when testing economic vs professional influence trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (organizational): broadcast sensitivity to profit
rubrics_metrics.description: Television and radio are more sensitive to profit needs than newspapers and magazines because virtually all broadcast income derives from advertisers and programming decisions have direct economic ramifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare media types for advertiser-driven programming/content differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (organizational): business-background managers favor economics
rubrics_metrics.description: Upper-level media managers with business-side backgrounds are more likely to make decisions based on economics rather than professional considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect manager background data to predict decision priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (organizational): middle management aligns with org goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Middle-level management personnel are more closely attuned to organizational goals than lower-level personnel, producing tension between editorial and business sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate role conflicts and influence differentials across hierarchical levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (organizational): combined business/editor control favors business
rubrics_metrics.description: When editorial routines conflict with the need to make a profit, and if the same editor controls both business and editorial sides, editorial priorities will be given lower priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine governance structures that merge editorial and business control for content effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (organizational): higher-level staff have nonmedia ties
rubrics_metrics.description: Higher-ranking individuals in media organizations are more likely to have connections with nonmedia organizations (boards, civic roles), influencing content decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map cross-sector ties of top managers and test associations with coverage decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (organizational): owner attitudes reflected in content
rubrics_metrics.description: Owners' personal attitudes and values may be reflected in editorials, columns, news and features; owners can hire/fire and cause subtle slants as employees anticipate owner preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study owner ideology and personnel changes alongside content shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (organizational): absentee ownership reduces localism
rubrics_metrics.description: The further the owner lives from the organization, the less local news, editorials, and features the organization will transmit (absentee ownership common in chains).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess owner proximity and chain ownership effects on local coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (organizational): chain employment weakens community ties
rubrics_metrics.description: Media workers in chain-owned organizations form weaker attachments to the local community than those in independent organizations; chain employees move more often and are more loyal to the corporation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare staff mobility, community engagement, and editorial stances between chain and independent outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (organizational): chain homogeneity in endorsements
rubrics_metrics.description: Chain organizations are more likely to endorse presidential candidates than independents, and endorsements tend to be homogeneous across the chain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze endorsement patterns and internal incentives for homogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (links org↔extramedia): source adaptation increases favorable coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: The more sources know about and adapt to a media organization's routines (timing, format), the more likely they are to receive favorable coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study PR and source practices in relation to coverage outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (links org↔extramedia): advertising affects editorial space
rubrics_metrics.description: The more advertising a newspaper or magazine has, the more pages it will devote to editorial (nonadvertising) content because print media assume a proportion of pages will be advertising and the remainder editorial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track advertising/editorial page relationships; note this may vary by medium and market logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (links org↔extramedia): extramedia connections increase influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The more connections between extramedia organizations and media organizations (e.g., board interlocks), the more influence extramedia firms will have on content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map cross-organizational linkages and test their association with content decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (extramedia): source power predicts influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The more economic or political power a source has, the more likely he or she is to influence news reports (accessible staff, tailored information).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure source power attributes and bundling of PR resources in source–media influence studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (extramedia): official sources dominate issues more than events
rubrics_metrics.description: Although official sources dominate most news, their percentage is higher in stories about issues than in those about events because issues involve vested official interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate source composition between event- and issue-based stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (extramedia): criticism by interest groups leads to self-censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: The more critical an interest group is of media coverage, the more likely the media are to self-censor (including via advertiser-targeted boycotts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine cases of interest-group pressure and subsequent content adjustments or anticipatory self-censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (extramedia): slow news days increase PR-generated content
rubrics_metrics.description: The slower the news day, the more likely media content is to be generated by public relations practitioners, since journalists still must fill preset content quotas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare source origin (PR vs independent reporting) by news-day tempo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (extramedia): elite media set agenda for others
rubrics_metrics.description: The more coverage opinion-leading (elite) media give an issue/event, the more likely other media are to give subsequent coverage (agenda-setting among media).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze cascade effects from elite outlets to secondary media in issue salience studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (extramedia): audience targeting shapes content
rubrics_metrics.description: The more a media organization promotes itself within a target audience, the more its content will reflect the interests of that audience (e.g., niche penetration to audiences attractive to advertisers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use audience targeting and marketing strategies as predictors of content orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (extramedia): advertisers shape content
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers influence media content: the more advertisers support one kind of content, the more the media will offer it; advertisers can withdraw support to shape or delete content and may create content showcasing products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure advertiser pressures, withdrawal events, and advertiser-created content to assess influence mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (extramedia↔state): criticism triggers government control
rubrics_metrics.description: The more the mass media criticize a country's government (and the more sources/interest groups criticize the media), the more the government will try to control the media via financing, laws, licenses, manipulation of information release, and direct contacts with managers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine state-level reactions to critical media and pathways of control across political systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (extramedia): community characteristics shape content
rubrics_metrics.description: Community characteristics (market size, competition) influence content: larger markets generate more spontaneous/local news; the presence of a competing newspaper does not necessarily increase content diversity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate market and community metrics when modeling content diversity and localism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (extramedia): geographic breadth standardizes content
rubrics_metrics.description: The wider the geographic area a medium covers, the more standardized its content will be (broad messages appeal to varying interests, reducing innovation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare local vs regional/national media for standardization and risk-taking in content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (ideology): deviance coverage and stereotyping
rubrics_metrics.description: The more deviant people or events are, the more likely they are to be included in media content and to be stereotyped; media maintain social boundaries by marking approval/disapproval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure deviance labeling and stereotyping intensity as functions of perceived deviance and ideological context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (ideology): international prominence shapes foreign coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: The more political, economic, or cultural significance one country has for another, the more the former will appear in the latter's mass media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include measures of bilateral significance when analyzing foreign news salience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (ideology): objectivity routines absent outside controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists will not apply objective routines (such as balance) when subjects are outside legitimate controversy or are in areas of consensus or deviance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test differential application of objectivity norms by issue controversy level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (ideology): elites act collectively when core principles threatened
rubrics_metrics.description: Elites will respond to media as a class when core ideological principles are threatened; business actions may be more unified when capitalist values are attacked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study coordinated elite responses and their effect on media content and policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (ideology): elite connections produce ideological consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: The more closely media are connected to other elites (board interlocks, club memberships), the more media content will align with elite ideological viewpoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Link elite network measures to content ideology indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (ideology): repair of occupational paradigm violations
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations of occupational paradigms (anomalies) must be repaired to preserve the paradigm, especially when violations cross important ideological boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine mechanisms of corrective coverage, reinterpretation, or marginalization when paradigms are threatened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis (ideology): TV more ideologically charged than print
rubrics_metrics.description: On a given issue, television coverage will be more ideologically charged than print media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare ideological tone and framing across media platforms for the same issues.
